extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers, naturalists, and geologists interested in physical geography and volcanology
extracted.subtask_description: Expository treatment of volcanic phenomena and rock classification: defines modes of rock origin, principal erupted-rock groups, stages and products of volcanic activity, and geographic/physical considerations bearing on volcanism. A 19th-century textbook-style overview intended to synthesize observation and theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rocks of eruption (erupted/endogenous rocks)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Rocks of eruption', which have issued from the interior of the earth either in a state of fusion from volcanic action, or in a more or less soft, viscous condition, from Plutonic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presented as one of four primary modes of origin. Later expanded into principal groups (granite & syenite, quartzose porphyry, greenstones/diorite). Erupted/endogenous rocks are contrasted with sedimentary/exogenous formations and metamorphic/transformed rocks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sedimentary rocks
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Sedimentary rocks', which have been precipitated and deposited on the earth's surface from a fluid, in which the most minute particles were either dissolved or held in suspension constituting the greater part of the secondary (or flotz) and tertiary groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the second of four modes of origin; examples and occurrences (travertine near Rome and Hobart Town, modern sea banks forming limestones) are given to illustrate ongoing sedimentary processes and human artifacts occasionally preserved in such deposits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformed or metamorphic rocks
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Transformed or metamorphic rocks', in which the internal texture and the mode of stratification have been changed, either by contact or proximity with a Plutonic or volcanic endogenous rock of eruption, or more frequently by a gaseous sublimation of substances which accompany certain masses erupted in a hot, fluid condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnote provides a detailed working definition of metamorphism (wide and narrow senses), examples of processes (discoloration by loss of carbon, conversion of anhydrite to gypsum, electro-chemical actions), and notes that some metamorphic processes remain mysterious; distinguishes metamorphism produced by internal (hypogene) agencies from surface weathering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conglomerates (mechanical/chemical precipitates and cemented detritus)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Conglomerates'; coarse or finely granular sandstones, or breccias composed of mechanically-divided masses of the three previous species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as the fourth mode of rock formation — by mechanical separation or chemical precipitation from liquids and by cementation of disintegrated heterogeneous rocks; examples and comparison to earlier chaotic formative processes are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal groups of erupted rocks: Granite and Syenite
rubrics_metrics.description: Granite and syenite of very different respective ages; granite frequently more recent, traversing syenite in veins and sometimes acting as the active upheaving agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes characteristic forms (insulated ellipsoidal masses, shell-cleft crust, concentric scaling), occurrences worldwide (Altai, Mysore, Lower Peru, Siberia) and relations to other rocks (superposed on slate, Jura limestone). Footnotes cite examples and authors (Bernhard Cotta, Leop. von Buch).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal groups of erupted rocks: Quartzose Porphyry
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Quartzose porphyry' is often found in the relation of veins to other rocks; base generally finely granular mixture of the same elements as larger embedded crystals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes textural relations (feldspathic base, granular and laminated in quartz-poor granitic porphyry) and references (Dufrenoy & Elie de Beaumont).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal groups of erupted rocks: Greenstones and Diorite
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Greenstones, Diorite', are granular mixtures of white albite and blackish-green hornblende, forming dioritic porphyry when the crystals are deposited in a base of denser tissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of the principal groups of endogenous/erupted rocks; presented as a textural/mineralogical definition rather than strict genetic rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages of volcanic activity characterized by distinctive products
rubrics_metrics.description: Every stage of volcanic activity, from origin to extinction, is characterized by peculiar products: first ignited scoriae, lava streams (trachyte, pyroxene, obsidian), lapilli and tufaceous ashes with large quantities of pure aqueous vapor; subsequently solfataras with aqueous vapors mixed with sulphureted hydrogen and carbonic acid gases; finally, when cooled, exhalations of carbonic acid alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a diagnostic framework to identify the stage of a volcanic field. Examples and contrasts between stages (lava-emitting vs. solfatara vs. cooled/extinct emissions) are provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dome-shaped elevations (craters of elevation) formed by vesicular distension
rubrics_metrics.description: Dome-shaped elevations (e.g., Methone) arise when vapours enclosed in dark caverns seek a passage; the heavier earth, inflated by the force of compressed vapours, expands and rises like a bladder, producing a tumulus once a plain and now a mountain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classified as a distinct phenomenon from eruptive volcanoes; classical descriptions (Ovid, Aristotle, Strabo) are cited to support the vesicular-distension mechanism and to distinguish such elevations from eruptive craters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity to the sea is not an absolute requirement for volcanic activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Although many active volcanoes are littoral and the sea has been invoked as feeding volcanic fires, observations show active volcanoes at great distances inland (e.g., Pe-schan in Thianschan many hundreds to over a thousand miles from seas), suggesting vicinity of the sea is not absolutely necessary for eruptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discusses historical hypotheses (penetration of sea water to volcanic foci) and counter-evidence drawn from geographic distribution; notes littoral situations favor eruptions by forming margins of deep sea basins offering less resistance, but do not constitute a necessary condition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypothesis of sea (or meteoric) water penetration and role of vapor pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: The aqueous vapours exhaled from volcanoes may be derived from sea water impregnated with salt or from fresh meteoric water; whether vapour expansive force at depth can counterbalance hydrostatic sea pressure and gain access to the focus is discussed, and steam/smoke eruptions are noted when vapour pressure exceeds hydrostatic pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Footnotes cite Gay-Lussac and Bischof and give examples (Lancerote, Iceland, Kurile Islands) where eruptions of steam and smoke during neighbouring eruptions indicate reaction through tense columns of water; this serves as a physical criterion for when water participates in volcanic phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extinction of volcanic activity: partial vs total and redistribution of subterranean fire
rubrics_metrics.description: Extinction may be partial — subterranean fire seeks another passage of escape in the same mountain chain — or total (complete cooling), as illustrated by examples (Auvergne, Mosychlos, Medina).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to interpret the present state of volcanism in a region; historical and geological evidence (legendary and recorded extinctions) are invoked to show different extinction modes and their consequences (e.g., swallowed-up craters, reefs indicating former activity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-lava igneous phenomena: hot-water and mud eruptions
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists a remarkable class of igneous mountains which do not eject lava but emit devastating streams of hot water impregnated with burning sulphur and rocks reduced to dust (example: Galungung in Java); eruptions of argillaceous mud, lodazales, and similar phenomena are comparable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes uncertainty whether these represent a normal condition or a transitory modification of volcanic process; calls for further geologists with knowledge of modern chemistry to determine the nature. Examples from Quito plateau and Java are cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volcanic forces as agents forming new rocks and transforming existing ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Volcanic action should be regarded not merely as a disturbing subterranean force but as forming new rocks and transforming those that already existed; this links mineralogical geognosy with the study of geographic forms and outlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framed as a methodological/principled stance: studying volcanic activity yields insight both into the mineralogical branch (texture/succession of strata) and into the configuration of continents and islands; supports an integrated philosophical approach to geognosy.
